title: Job again
hookLine: God never explains, but shows up, and Job's friends are rebuked

cards: The casseroles arrive first. Then the cards. Then the explanations.
Everything happens for a reason. At least it was quick. It must have been their time.
People mean well. They want to fill a silence that feels unbearable. Back in year two, this path spent a run of days in the book of Job.
Today it comes back with one question: what does Job teach about being there for someone who's suffering?

teach.b: Start with what the friends got right. They came: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great."

Some readers say the friends never comforted Job better than in that silent week. Then they started talking. Their speeches circle one idea: God is just, so if you're suffering, you must have done something.
Job's reply is sharp: "miserable comforters are ye all." He had already told them what would help: "O that ye would altogether hold your peace! and it should be your wisdom."
Then God speaks, out of the whirlwind. You'd expect the explanation at last, the scene in heaven from the first chapter. God never mentions it.
Instead God asks questions: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?" Not an answer: an encounter. Job, who demanded a hearing, gets one, and goes quiet.
Last, the rebuke. God tells Eliphaz, one of the friends: "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath."
The friends with their tidy explanations are corrected; Job, who wept and argued and accused, is said to have spoken rightly.
Some readers notice the shape: God didn't explain, but showed up; the friends explained, and were rebuked. Explaining feels like helping.
Read this way, the book suggests that sitting beside someone, saying nothing, may be the more faithful thing.
And if you're the one grieving and ever feel in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

how: Some Christians turn to Job when they or someone close to them is suffering, and some pastors and chaplains point to the friends' silent week, and their later rebuke, as a pattern for visiting the grieving: be present, and resist explaining.

games.q: you're Job. you've lost almost everything, and you've demanded a hearing. now God answers out of the whirlwind. what do you hear?
o: the reason for it all: the scene in heaven from the first chapter.
questions about the making of the world.
that your friends were right about you.
games.why: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?" God never mentions the scene in heaven. no explanation, but an encounter.

practice: Bring to mind someone going through something hard, notice the urge to fix it or find the perfect sentence, and set it down.
Then picture one simple way to be there: a visit, a meal left at the door, a message that says only I'm thinking of you, an hour beside them in the quiet.
If you pray, you can hold them before God without asking for an explanation; if you don't, hold them in mind, the way the friends sat on the ground.
